---
title: "Great Tables Integration"
---

Gridwell integrates with [Great Tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/) to render
GT objects to all 11 output formats from Python.

## Installation

The Great Tables integration needs the optional `gt` extra (Great Tables and pandas):

```bash
pip install 'gridwell[gt]'
```

Without it, `import gridwell` still works. Calling `gridwell.gt_to_ir` then raises an
`ImportError` that explains how to install the extra.

## Quick Start

```python
from great_tables import GT, exibble
import gridwell

gt = GT(exibble.head(5), rowname_col="row", groupname_col="group")

table = gridwell.Table(gt)  # converts the GT to gridwell's IR
html = table.render_html()
```

`gridwell.Table()` (or `gridwell.Table.from_gt()`, which takes only a GT) converts the
table to IR. In a notebook (Jupyter, VS Code, Quarto) a `Table` shows as HTML, with
styles scoped to that one table and marked so Quarto doesn't add Bootstrap's table
styling; `print(table)` draws it as text, and `repr(table)` describes it:

```python
>>> table
<gridwell.Table: 8 columns, 5 rows in 2 groups>
```

## Functions

### `gridwell.gt_to_ir(gt, emitter="auto")`

Converts a Great Tables `GT` object to gridwell IR JSON string.

```python
ir_json = gridwell.gt_to_ir(gt)  # returns str (JSON)
```

### `gridwell.gt_to_dict(gt, emitter="auto")`

Converts a GT object to a Python dict (IR structure).

```python
ir_dict = gridwell.gt_to_dict(gt)  # returns dict
```

### Which converter

The converter is moving into Great Tables, as `GT.as_ir()`, since it reads Great
Tables' internals and Great Tables can keep it in step with them. Until every Great
Tables has it, gridwell keeps its own copy. `emitter` picks one:

- `"auto"` (the default): Great Tables' when the installed Great Tables has
  `GT.as_ir()`, and gridwell's otherwise. If Great Tables' raises, or gives an IR major
  version this gridwell can't read, gridwell's is used with a `UserWarning` saying why.
- `"upstream"`: Great Tables', raising if there is none or it can't be used.
- `"gridwell"`: gridwell's.

Great Tables' own needs no pandas (a table on polars converts as it is); gridwell's
needs pandas, from the `gt` extra. No released Great Tables has `GT.as_ir()` yet, so
today `"auto"` always uses gridwell's.

## What Gets Converted

| GT Feature | IR Mapping |
|------------|-----------|
| Column labels | `thead` rows |
| Spanners (`tab_spanner()`, any number of levels) | `spanner_label` rows above the column labels, drawn as Great Tables draws them |
| Row groups | `tbody` array with group labels |
| Stub column | Cells with `is_stub: true` and `scope: "row"` (row headers, as in Great Tables' HTML), always aligned left |
| A stub of several columns (`rowname_col=["region", "city"]`) | One stub column each, outermost first. Where an outer column's value is the same in consecutive rows of a group (and so are the columns to its left), the rows share one cell spanning them (`rowspan`, `scope: "rowgroup"`), merged in the order the rows are shown |
| Row group column (`tab_options(row_group_as_column=True)`) | The first stub column: each group's label is a stub cell spanning its rows (`scope: "rowgroup"`), and the group has no label row |
| Stubhead label (`tab_stubhead()`) | One head cell spanning the stub columns (blank without one); a list of labels (`tab_stubhead(["A", "B"])`) gives each row stub column its own, with a blank one above a row group column |
| Summary rows (`summary_rows()`, `grand_summary_rows()`) | A group's `summary_rows`, and a last group without a label for the grand summary; a table without a stub gets an empty one for their labels, as in Great Tables. A group whose summary rows are all on its top side (`side="top"`) has them at the top (`summary_placement: "top"`); one with rows on both sides has them all at the bottom, after its rows. Grand summary rows on the top side are a first group without a label, with its rows at the top. With a row group column, a summary row's label spans the other stub columns, beside an empty cell under the group's label (Great Tables' HTML has the group's cell span its summary rows instead) |
| Title/subtitle | `header` block |
| Source notes | `footer.source_notes` |
| Footnotes (`tab_footnote()`) | `footer.footnotes`, the ones Great Tables lists, in its order and with its marks; each mark is also on the cell or label it annotates, where Great Tables puts it (with `placement="auto"`, before a number and after anything else) |
| Styles (`tab_style()`) | Each styled cell's or label's own style (`style_id`), as the CSS Great Tables writes for it, later declarations winning: text, fill, borders and the `style.css()` declarations the IR has. A font size without a unit (`style.text(size=12)`) is in pixels; properties the IR has no equivalent for (`font-stretch`, `letter-spacing`) are dropped |
| Table options (`tab_options()`, `opt_stylize()`, `opt_row_striping()`) | The options the IR can express, where changed from Great Tables' defaults: the fills (with the text color Great Tables gives them) and font weights of the column labels, row group labels and stub, the summary rows' fills, no lines between body rows, striping (a conditional style on even rows, of the stub, the body or both), and the table's borders (below). Other options (fonts, sizes, padding, vertical lines between body cells) aren't converted yet |
| `md()` and `html()` labels | The content of the HTML Great Tables makes of them: text with bold, italic, underline, strike-through and code runs, line breaks, superscripts and subscripts in Unicode characters where every character has one (`m²`), images (`<img>`, their `src` copied, never read) and SVG as raw HTML (other markup is dropped and its text kept) |
| Column alignment | `column_spec[].align` |
| Column widths | `column_spec[].width` |
| Formatted values | Cell `content`: the content of the HTML Great Tables puts in the cell, read as labels are, so `fmt_*()` output that is HTML (`fmt_markdown()`, `fmt_units()`, `fmt_scientific()`, `fmt_image()`, nanoplots) is drawn as formatted, and other values are their text. |
| Typed values | Cell `typed_value` (below) |

A cell's [typed value](../schema/table-data.qmd#typed-values) is what a spreadsheet
holds, so XLSX keeps numbers, booleans, dates and times as values, each shown as the
table shows it:

- A number is the number displayed (`0.11` for `0.1111` formatted to two decimals),
  as the R package does for gt tables: in any locale's marks (`1234.5` for
  `1.234,50` and `1 234,50`), with its currency or unit left out (`49.95` for
  `$49.95`, `1234.5` for `1,234.50 kg`), a sign or accounting parentheses (`-5` for
  `($5.00)`), as a fraction for a percentage or per mille (`0.451` for `45.1%`), and
  scaled for scientific and compact notation (`0.000123` for `1.23 × 10⁻⁴`,
  `1230000` for `1.23M`). A display with one mark (`1,234`) is read as the data's
  value rounds to it (a thousand and more, or a little more than one); one read
  only one way is read so even when the value doesn't round to it (a value scaled
  with `scale_by=`). A display that isn't one number (`<0.001`, `46 (37, 60)`,
  `4/9`) has none, so the cell stays text.
- Booleans, and `datetime.date`, `datetime.datetime` (or pandas `Timestamp`) and
  `datetime.time` values are typed; a date or time is written without its time
  zone, as the wall-clock time the table shows. Dates held as strings stay strings.

## Language and direction

A table given a locale (`GT(df, locale="ar_EG")`) is in that language: the IR's
`config.locale` and [`config.lang`](../schema/config.qmd#language-and-direction) are
the locale as a language tag (`ar-EG`). When the language is written right to left
(Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu and the like, or any language in a right-to-left
script such as `pa_Arab`), `config.dir` is `rtl`, so the columns and text run right
to left. Great Tables' own HTML stays left to right. A table without a locale gets
neither `lang` nor `dir`, as before.

The R package does the same for gt's `locale` (`gt(df, locale = "ar")`).

## Borders

The border options (`table_border_*`, `heading_border_bottom_*`,
`column_labels_border_*`, `row_group_border_*`, `table_body_border_*`,
`table_body_hlines_*`, `stub_border_*`, `summary_row_border_*` and
`grand_summary_row_border_*`) become the table's
[rules](../schema/config.qmd#rules), where changed from Great Tables' defaults. Each
rule takes the style, width and color of the options that draw it in Great Tables'
HTML. Where two options draw one rule, the outer one's changes win: with a heading,
`table_border_top_*` is the rule above it (`title`) and `heading_border_bottom_*`
and `column_labels_border_top_*` the one under it (`top`); without one,
`table_border_top_*` is `top`. The same goes for `table_border_bottom_*`, which is
the rule under the footer (`notes`), or the table's `bottom` when there is no
footer. Styles the IR has no rule for (`groove`, `ridge`, `inset`, `outset`) are
left out.

## HTML ids

The HTML writer gives the header cells the ids Great Tables gives them, and each
body cell the same `headers` (except that stub cells are numbered in the order the
rows are shown, where Great Tables numbers them by data row, which differs when row
groups reorder the rows). Great Tables' `GT(id=)` is the table's
[`config.id`](../schema/config.qmd), which the HTML writer uses as its `table_id`, so
the ids are prefixed as Great Tables prefixes them:

```python
gt = GT(exibble, rowname_col="row", groupname_col="group", id="sales")
html = gridwell.Table(gt).render_html()  # ids start "sales-"
```

The writer's `table_id` option, when set, is used instead. An id that isn't an HTML
id (empty, or with whitespace) is left out.

## Full Pipeline Example

```python
from great_tables import GT, exibble
import gridwell

gt = (
    GT(exibble, rowname_col="row", groupname_col="group")
    .tab_header(title="Example Table", subtitle="From exibble")
    .tab_source_note(source_note="Source: great_tables package")
)

# Convert and validate
table = gridwell.Table(gt)
errors = table.validate()
assert errors == []

# Render all text formats
for fmt in ["html", "latex", "typst", "rtf", "svg", "ansi", "pandoc", "quarto"]:
    output = table.render(fmt)
    print(f"{fmt}: {len(output)} chars")

# Render binary formats
for fmt in ["docx", "xlsx", "pptx"]:
    data = table.render_binary(fmt)
    print(f"{fmt}: {len(data)} bytes")
```
